rationale: B wins because its best angles are more assignment-ready: it turns the company claims into testable reporting questions, especially “Half the prep time: what a guacamole robot actually does to a lunch rush.” A is clean and safer, but “Inside the kitchen where a robot halved the time it takes to make guac” is the same operations story with less pressure on the baseline. B nearly hands the win back with its Digital Makeline overreach, but its proof demands are sharper where the real press risk lives.
gaps_in_A: “The prevailing belief right now is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu” is plausible, but it is not in the update; A needs that sourced or softened.
“Inside the kitchen where a robot halved the time it takes to make guac” lets “roughly halves” carry too much weight; the stronger angle is the missing baseline behind the number.

“What Chipotle's robots mean for investors and the stock” is misfiled as `hallucinated_fact`; the investor/margin question is legitimate, just unpitchable without labor costs, unit economics, or analyst context.
A leaves the data angle underbuilt. “The actual before/after prep-time numbers behind ‘roughly halves’” should not be buried only as proof; it is the heart of the operations story.
gaps_in_B: “first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format” is an overclaim; the update says one robot is rolling out and another is testing, not that Chipotle has automated the full line.
“the two statements were made together and can only be examined together right now” is stronger than the facts allow; the update gives both facts, not the announcement packaging.
“Other operators watching this decide their own capex from it” invents market consequence. A reporter might ask that, but B cannot state it as the reason the story matters.
“Next step: `newsjack-detector`” is the wrong default from a same-day company update; proof gathering and `journalist-fit-check` come first unless there is an actual external news peg to test.
